problems.title: PAZO-M step size allows an exact nonstationary two-cycle
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Theorem 4.1, p. 6; Theorem B.3, p. 16; proof condition before Eq. (11), p. 18.
claim: Theorem 4.1/Theorem B.3 assert a finite-time stationarity bound for the prescribed PAZO-M step size without the restriction later used in the proof.
analysis: Choose \(d=q=b=b'=1\), identical public/private per-record losses \(f(x)=1-\cos x\), \(L=M=1\), \(\alpha=0.9\), \(\lambda=10^{-6}\), and zero gradient-variance, similarity and injected-noise parameters. The objective is smooth, Lipschitz, bounded below and bounded in \([0,2]\). Clipping is inactive because the threshold is \(1+\sqrt2\) while the scalar directional derivative has magnitude at most one.

The prescribed step is \(\eta=2.75\). For \(u\in\{-1,1\}\), using \(\operatorname{sinc}(\lambda)=\sin\lambda/\lambda\), the two-point estimator is \(\operatorname{sinc}(\lambda)\sin x\), so the exact recurrence is \(x_{t+1}=x_t-a\sin x_t\), with \(a=\eta[\alpha+(1-\alpha)\operatorname{sinc}(\lambda)]\in(2.7,2.75)\). A nonzero root \(a\sin x_0=2x_0\) lies in \((\pi/3,\pi/2)\); hence \(x_t=(-1)^t x_0\) and \(|\nabla f(x_t)|^2>3/4\).

At \(T=1000\), the complete surviving right side of Theorem B.3 is \(\frac{16(1-\cos x_0)(1-\alpha)}{T(2-\alpha)^2}+\frac{2\lambda(1-\alpha)}{2-\alpha}+\frac{\lambda^2(1-\alpha)}4+\frac{\alpha\lambda}2<0.001324\). It cannot bound a left side greater than \(3/4\). In particular, the proof condition \(\alpha L\eta<1\) fails: its value is \(2.475\).
result: The finite-time theorem is false on its stated domain. This is an analytic cycle, not an empirical training failure. The distinct bounded-loss Theorem B.6 already restricts \(\alpha<2/3\) and is not refuted by this example.
repair: State and enforce \(\alpha L\eta<1\), or cap the step and rederive the bound. With \(s=\sqrt d\), the prescribed step satisfies this condition when \(\alpha<(4s-1-\sqrt{4s^2+1})/(3s-2)\); \(0<\alpha<2/3\) suffices uniformly in dimension. This repairs the exhibited obstruction without recertifying every intermediate line.
problems.impact_rationale: A bounded smooth admissible objective gives an exact nonstationary cycle violating the full finite-time theorem. This directly damages a central convergence guarantee.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: PAZO-S selection invalidates unconditional moment substitutions
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Theorem B.5 proof, pp. 23-24 (selected batch moments and accepted Gaussian perturbation).
claim: Theorem B.5's proof treats a privately selected public-gradient candidate as if its pre-selection moments and zero-mean perturbation were unchanged.
analysis: Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}\) and public per-example loss \(f(x)+\zeta x\), with \(\Pr(\zeta=0.2)=0.01\) and \(\Pr(\zeta=-0.2/99)=0.99\). At \(x=1\), step \(1/4\), three public candidates and exact private comparisons, both candidate positions are positive; minimizing private loss selects the largest \(\zeta\). Thus \(\mathbb E\zeta=0\), but \(\mathbb E\zeta_I=0.00398\), and the selected second moment is about \(2.9502\) times the unselected \(0.0004040404\).

Zero-mean Gaussian perturbations also become biased under acceptance. For one exact public gradient, put \(y=1-1/(4\sqrt2)>0\), \(Z\sim N(0,\epsilon_p^2)\), and \(\eta=1/4\). Acceptance occurs exactly when \(0<Z<2y/\eta\), so \(\mathbb E[Z\mathbf1_A]=\epsilon_p[\phi(0)-\phi(2y/(\eta\epsilon_p))]>0\), where \(\phi\) is the standard-normal density.
result: These are counterexamples to the proof's moment substitutions. They do not by themselves refute the complete finite-time inequality, because a different descent argument could exploit selection.
repair: A selection-safe bound uses \(\mathbb E\|\zeta_I\|^2\le\sum_{j=1}^k\mathbb E\|\zeta_j\|^2\le k\sigma_2^2/b'\). With \(\eta=1/(4L)\), smoothness then yields \(\frac1T\sum_t\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_t)\|^2\le8L\Delta_f/T+(\gamma+\sqrt{k\sigma_2^2/b'}+\sqrt d\,\epsilon_p)^2\). This conservative replacement does not certify the paper's sharper dependence.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Fixed PAZO-S perturbations do not give a vanishing asymptotic error
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Eq. (6) and asymptotic paragraph, p. 7; Theorem B.5 and its asymptotic sentence, p. 23.
claim: The asymptotic paragraph after Eq. (\(6\))/Theorem B.5 claims an \(O(\gamma^2+\sigma_2^2/b')\) error from \(T\to\infty\) and \(\epsilon_p\le d^{-1/2}\), dropping terms retained in the finite-time display.
analysis: A fixed positive perturbation does not vanish. Take \(d=k=b=b'=1\), identical losses \(f=f'=1-\cos x\), \(\eta=1/4\), \(\epsilon_p=1\), clipping threshold \(C=2\) and private-noise multiplier \(\sigma\ge1\). Here \(\gamma=\sigma_2=0\). The baseline candidate is \(y=x-\eta\sin x\), and its perturbed competitor is \(y+W\), with \(W\sim N(0,1/16)\).

Since each true loss is in \([0,2]\), the perturbed candidate is accepted with conditional probability at least \(\Phi(-1/(2\sigma))\ge\Phi(-1/2)>0\). On every interval of length \(\pi\), the set where \(\sin^2(y+w)\ge1/2\) has measure \(\pi/2\). The Gaussian density is uniformly positive on \([-\pi/2,\pi/2]\). Therefore \(\mathbb E[|\nabla f(x_{t+1})|^2\mid x_t]\ge\frac12\Phi(-1/2)\frac\pi2\,\frac{\phi(2\pi)}{1/4}\simeq1.0345190\times10^{-9}>0\), uniformly in \(x_t\).
result: The asymptotic zero-error conclusion is false when its right side is zero. The finite-time theorem retaining \(+1/2\) is not disproved by this example.
repair: Retain the \(d\epsilon_p^2\) contribution and selection-safe variance terms. A vanishing perturbation floor requires, for example, \(\epsilon_p=O((dT)^{-1/2})\), or no perturbation.
problems.impact_rationale: A uniform positive gradient floor contradicts the advertised asymptotic zero-error conclusion even with identical public/private objectives and zero public variance.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Conditioning on no clipping destroys the isotropy identity
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Theorem B.7, pp. 30-33; terms T1, p. 31, and T4, p. 32.
claim: Theorem B.7's proof uses an unconditional isotropy/projection identity after conditioning on the directional queries not clipping.
analysis: The no-clipping event depends on the sampled direction. For \(G=I_2\), \(g=e_1\), \(u\) uniform on the radius-\(\sqrt2\) circle and \(Q=\{|u_1|\le1\}\), direct angular integration gives \(\Pr(Q)=1/2\) and \(\mathbb E[uu^\top\mid Q]=\operatorname{diag}(1-2/\pi,1+2/\pi)\). Consequently \(\mathbb E[GG^\top g-(g^\top Gu)Gu\mid Q]=(2/\pi)e_1\ne0\). The threshold illustrates the conditioning error; it is not asserted to be the optimized threshold in Theorem B.7.
result: Conditional isotropy needs a separate proof or a clipping-bias remainder. The full optimized convergence rate has not been disproved.
repair: Work unconditionally. If \(Y^c\) is the clipped estimator, \(Y\) the unclipped estimator and \(p_t=\Pr(Q_t^c\mid\text{past})\), use \(\|\mathbb E(Y^c-Y)\|\le Mk p_t\) and \(\mathbb E\|Y^c\|^2\le2\mathbb E\|Y\|^2+2M^2k^2p_t\), then retain and bound the tail terms. The available replacement restricts to one direction and orthonormal \(G\).
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The smoothing variable in Lemma B.2 must be a ball draw
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Lemma B.2(3), p. 15; ball-smoothing definition, p. 3.
claim: Lemma B.2 uses sphere smoothing in a formula requiring ball smoothing.
analysis: In dimension one, sphere smoothing of \(f(x)=\sin x\) gives gradient \(\cos(\lambda)\cos x\). The mean symmetric two-point estimator is \(\operatorname{sinc}(\lambda)\cos x\). These differ for general \(\lambda\), whereas uniform ball smoothing gives the required estimator identity.
result: Local correctable error, not evidence that every smoothing argument fails.
repair: Use the uniform ball expectation, consistent with the main-text definition.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: MNLI vectorized PAZO-S uses candidate parameters as gradients
problems.source_location: Official supplement and pinned pinned author GitHub source: mnli/pazo-s_vec.py, lines 150-164.
claim: The vectorized candidate-selection branch should update the parameters corresponding to the candidate it evaluates.
analysis: The winning candidate variable best_g_noise contains parameters \(\theta-\eta(g+z)\), but the source assigns that value to p.grad before optimizer.step(). It therefore uses a candidate position as a gradient; that update does not generally equal the candidate evaluated by the private comparison.
result: The parameter actually updated differs from the candidate whose private loss won the selection. Defect is file-specific and present in both audited versions.
repair: Represent candidate gradient and candidate parameters separately. Assign g+z to p.grad and evaluate the candidate consistent with the actual optimizer; if assigning parameters directly, reconcile momentum and weight-decay state.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.

problems.title: The implemented sampler is not the accountant's mechanism
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Section 3.4, pp. 5-6. pinned author GitHub source: trainers/model_base.py, lines 149-251; privacy_analysis/compute_privacy_sgm.py, lines 8-51; privacy_analysis/rdp_accountant.py, lines 355-399.
claim: The reported differential-privacy accounting is used with the author-released training sampler.
analysis: The author's fixed-size DataLoader uses shuffled epochs and drops the last incomplete batch. Its compute_rdp helper instead accounts for a sampled Gaussian mixture at \(q=b/n\). Epoch reshuffling is not that sampling mechanism; even independent fresh fixed-size batches would be a different rule. The code contains a separate without-replacement helper but does not use it on this path.
result: The displayed accounting does not establish the released loop's stated budgets. This is a certification-scope gap, not a proved numerical privacy violation. Counting all nominal epoch steps is conservative relative to dropping incomplete batches.
repair: Use independent Poisson inclusion with fixed public expected-batch normalization and explicit empty-batch behavior, or supply a matching reshuffling accountant and adjacency analysis. Recompute budgets and handle PAZO-S's adaptive final query/shared batch explicitly.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Private-derived preprocessing and diagnostics expand the privacy boundary
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Appendix C.1, p. 34. pinned author GitHub source: data/generate_imdb_vocab10k.py, lines 36-56 and 85-124; experiments/pazo-s.py, lines 148-153.
claim: The privacy interpretation must specify which preprocessing-dependent models and diagnostic outputs are released.
analysis: Deterministic top-token vocabulary is built from private training text, saved, and used for all datasets. Training code writes raw private accuracy and candidate diagnostics; data preparation prints decoded private examples.
result: The stated scalar mechanism does not protect the whole raw-record preprocessing/output pipeline. Conditional DP for fixed preprocessed examples is a narrower possible claim.
repair: Fix a public tokenizer independently of protected records, or privately construct it with composed budget. Define the released object; privatize or exclude raw private diagnostics and data artifacts. Address private model selection and multiple released runs where applicable.

problems.title: The historical PAZO-M public-norm scaling has been corrected
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Algorithm 1, p. 4; Appendix A, p. 14; implementation disclosure, p. 34. Supplement and pinned author GitHub source: experiments/pazo-m.py, lines 85-90; mnli/pazo-m.py, lines 126-131.
claim: The older conference supplement scaled Gaussian search directions by the public-gradient norm. The latest author repository uses a different dimension-dependent scale.
analysis: The older public-norm rule has conditional mean \((\|g_{\rm pub}\|^2/d)\nabla f\), whereas the checked current author release uses \(Z/d^{1/4}\) in experiments/pazo-m.py and the corresponding MNLI implementation. Freshly retrieved current files confirm that the historical norm-dependent scaling is absent. This comparison identifies a code revision; it does not identify the revision used by the published runs.
result: The particular historical scaling defect is cleared as a current-source allegation. The current implementation and the original experimental provenance must remain separate.
problems.impact_rationale: No current-error impact is assigned to this corrected historical implementation concern.
problems.existing_correction_status: The current author repository already removes the historical public-norm scaling; this does not establish adoption of this audit.

problems.title: Fixed seeds and test-based stopping do not establish significance
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Appendix C.2, p. 34, and statistical-significance checklist, p. 43. pinned author GitHub source: experiments/pazo-s_vec.py, lines 62-92; mnli/pazo-s.py, lines 86-116.
claim: The paper uses fixed-seed and hyperparameter stability observations to discuss significance.
analysis: Paper acknowledges seed \(0\) and no error bars but claims significance from fixed seed and hyperparameter stability. Several code paths use test_accu for patience-based stopping.
result: Small reported advantages, especially \(0.2\) percentage points on Tiny-ImageNet at \(\varepsilon=0.1\), have no established statistical significance. Magnitude of selection bias is not quantified.
repair: Use multiple independent seeds, paired per-seed comparisons and uncertainty; choose configurations/stopping on a validation split and evaluate once on a separate final holdout. Label existing results single-seed measurements.

problems.title: The IMDB speedup ratio and timing interpretation
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Section 5.3, pp. 9-10; Tables 8-9, pp. 36-37. pinned author GitHub source: experiments/pazo-s.py, lines 138-145.
claim: The paper reports an IMDB speedup of up to fifteen times the comparison baseline.
analysis: IMDB largest baseline \(0.252\) seconds divided by fastest PAZO \(0.019\) is \(13.263\), not \(15\). Rounding cannot bridge the difference. Timing covers \(20\) iterations and does not specify explicit accelerator synchronization/warmup in the measurement code.
result: CIFAR up-to-\(16\times\) relative to GEP is supported by the table; not all runtime claims fail. No GPU performance reproduction was conducted.
repair: Correct the IMDB ratio or publish the missing underlying timing that justifies it. Name the baseline for each speedup. Report synchronized repeated timings, warmup/compile treatment and end-to-end time to matched utility. Measure actual peak memory for memory claims.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
